document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer develops two weeks of progressive mid-thoracic back pain, now with bilateral leg weakness, a T8 sensory level, and urinary retention. MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrates a destructive T8 vertebral body lesion with an adjacent soft tissue mass indenting and compressing the spinal cord. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Extradural metastatic tumour compressing the cord

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes classifies spinal tumours by compartment: extradural lesions account for about 55% of all spinal tumours and are typically metastases from lymphoma, lung, breast, or prostate. This man has a known prostate primary with a destructive vertebral body lesion and an epidural soft tissue mass, which is the classic extradural metastatic pattern producing cord compression.

optionExplanations.b: Meningioma is an intradural extramedullary tumour and does not destroy the vertebral body.
optionExplanations.c: Intradural intramedullary tumours such as ependymomas account for only about 5% of spinal tumours and arise within the cord itself, not from bone.
optionExplanations.d: Syringomyelia is a fluid-filled intramedullary cavity related to trauma or congenital or idiopathic causes, not a destructive bony lesion.
optionExplanations.e: Dural AVF is a vascular extradural cause of myelopathy and would not produce a destructive vertebral body mass.

source.reference: NS4 — Differential Diagnoses of Common Presentations (Table 1)

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman describes three months of headache that has become constant, progressively more severe, worst on waking, and that at times wakes her from sleep. Over the past two weeks she has had intermittent blurred vision and several episodes of forceful vomiting that occurred without preceding nausea. She is afebrile and alert with no neck stiffness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Intracranial tumour causing raised intracranial pressure

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes maps intracranial pathology to its time course: vascular causes are sudden, metabolic causes evolve over hours to days, infectious causes over days to weeks, and tumours over months. A tumour raises ICP and produces a constant, progressive, severe headache that is worse in the morning and may wake the patient, with blurry vision and projectile vomiting as ICP rises. This three-month course with exactly those features fits a tumour.

optionExplanations.b: Hemorrhagic vascular events present suddenly, not with a three-month progressive course.
optionExplanations.c: Metabolic causes evolve over hours to days and affect the entire CNS rather than producing isolated progressive morning headache.
optionExplanations.d: Infectious causes such as abscess typically develop over days to weeks and usually have a source of infection or immunodeficiency in the history; she is afebrile.
optionExplanations.e: Ischemic stroke is a sudden vascular event and is characteristically without headache.

source.reference: NS4 — Intracranial Pressure Dynamics (Table 2, Approach to Intracranial Pathology)

questions.question: A 71-year-old right-handed woman is brought to the emergency department because she has "stopped making sense." She speaks fluently and at a normal rate, but her sentences are well-formed and largely meaningless. She cannot follow simple one-step commands and cannot repeat a short phrase. Strength, tone, and reflexes are normal in all limbs. Which lesion location best accounts for these findings?

options.text: Posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
Posterior inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes localizes Wernicke's area to the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, and a lesion there produces a fluent aphasia with impaired repetition and impaired comprehension. This patient is fluent yet unable to comprehend commands or repeat, which is the Wernicke pattern rather than a motor or parietal syndrome.

optionExplanations.b: Broca's area lesions give a non-fluent, dysarthric aphasia with impaired repetition but spared comprehension.
optionExplanations.c: Non-dominant parietal lesions cause inattention or extinction of the non-dominant side, not fluent aphasia.
optionExplanations.d: Dominant parietal lesions cause aphasias and Gerstmann's syndrome, but the fluent-with-impaired-comprehension pattern localizes to posterior superior temporal cortex.
optionExplanations.e: Occipital lesions cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia without language disturbance.

source.reference: NS5 — Consequences of Common Brain Lesions (Table 3)

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman reports 18 months of gradually progressive right-sided hearing loss with increasing unsteadiness on her feet. On examination the right corneal reflex is reduced, there is mild right lower motor neuron facial weakness, hearing is diminished on the right, and she is ataxic with a tendency to veer to the right. Limb power, reflexes, and plantar responses are normal. Which location best accounts for this constellation?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that a cerebellopontine angle lesion produces disequilibrium, ataxia, and deficits of cranial nerves V, VII, and VIII. This woman has exactly that triad of cranial nerve findings (reduced corneal reflex, facial weakness, hearing loss) combined with imbalance, localizing to the right CPA.

optionExplanations.b: A cerebellar hemisphere lesion causes intention tremor, ipsilateral limb ataxia, and falling toward the side of the lesion, but not cranial nerve V, VII, and VIII deficits.
optionExplanations.c: Vermis lesions cause truncal ataxia and dysarthria without these cranial nerve findings.
optionExplanations.d: Dorsal midbrain and pineal lesions cause Parinaud's syndrome with supranuclear upward gaze palsy.
optionExplanations.e: A pontine lesion classically produces locked-in syndrome, and there are no long-tract signs here.

source.reference: NS5 — Consequences of Common Brain Lesions (Table 3)

questions.question: A 27-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle collision. He was intubated at the scene and his GCS is 6T. CT head shows bilateral frontal contusions with effacement of the basal cisterns. He is admitted to the ICU, and the neurosurgical team decides to monitor intracranial pressure, wanting the most accurate available measurement with the option of therapeutic CSF drainage. Which method is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists ICP monitoring as indicated in severe TBI with GCS <8T plus an abnormal CT, and identifies the intraventricular catheter (EVD) as the gold standard because it is the most accurate method and also allows therapeutic drainage of CSF. This patient meets the indication and needs both accurate measurement and drainage capability.

optionExplanations.b: A parenchymal monitor is an accepted alternative but is not the gold standard and cannot drain CSF.
optionExplanations.c: An epidural monitor is a listed device but is less accurate and offers no therapeutic drainage.
optionExplanations.d: Serial LP is not the most accurate method and is absolutely contraindicated with suspected acutely raised ICP because it can precipitate tonsillar and uncal herniation.
optionExplanations.e: Non-invasive methods such as transcranial Doppler do not measure ICP accurately enough for routine monitoring.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman with a large left frontal glioma and several days of worsening headache becomes agitated and hypoxic in the emergency department. Her intracranial pressure is presumed to be elevated, and rapid sequence intubation is planned. The team specifically wants to avoid any agent whose drug-induced muscle fasciculations could transiently raise intracranial pressure further. Which of the following agents is best avoided?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists succinylcholine among the medications to use with caution in elevated ICP because the fasciculations it induces may increase ICP. In a patient with a large intracranial mass and presumed raised ICP, this is the agent to avoid on that specific mechanistic basis.

optionExplanations.b: Rocuronium is a non-depolarizing blocker and does not produce fasciculations.
optionExplanations.c: Vecuronium is non-depolarizing and is not listed as a cautioned agent in elevated ICP.
optionExplanations.d: Cisatracurium is non-depolarizing and does not cause fasciculations.
optionExplanations.e: Etomidate is an induction agent, not a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, and does not act through fasciculations.

source.reference: NS6 — Cautioned Medication Use in Elevated ICP

questions.question: A 22-year-old man struck his head in a fall, was briefly unconscious, then spoke normally with paramedics. Ninety minutes later he becomes progressively drowsy. His right pupil is 6 mm and non-reactive, with right ptosis and impaired right extraocular movements. He has left-sided weakness with an upgoing left plantar response. CT shows a large right-sided extradural hematoma. Which herniation syndrome best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes uncal (lateral tentorial) herniation as arising from a lateral supratentorial lesion, often a rapidly expanding traumatic hematoma, with an ipsilateral non-reactive dilated pupil as the earliest and most reliable sign, plus ipsilateral extraocular paralysis and ptosis from CN III compression, decreased LOC, and contralateral hemiplegia with an extensor plantar response. This patient's rapidly expanding right extradural hematoma has produced precisely that pattern.

optionExplanations.b: Subfalcine herniation is usually asymptomatic and warns of impending transtentorial herniation; it does not cause a blown pupil.
optionExplanations.c: Central tentorial herniation arises from a midline supratentorial lesion and gives small, fixed pupils with sequential diencephalic and medullary failure.
optionExplanations.d: Upward herniation follows a posterior fossa mass or cerebellar infarct, not a lateral supratentorial hematoma.
optionExplanations.e: Tonsillar herniation follows infratentorial lesions or LP with a mass lesion, causing neck stiffness, flaccid paralysis, and respiratory arrest.

questions.question: A 36-year-old woman reports eight weeks of headache that is worse in the morning and aggravated by coughing and stooping, with brief episodic "grey-outs" of vision lasting about 20 minutes. Fundoscopy shows bilateral optic disc swelling with blurred margins. She has a new left abducens palsy but is alert, with no limb weakness. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: Her headache aggravated by stooping and coughing, obvious papilledema with episodic visual field constrictions lasting about 20 minutes, and a CN VI palsy are the features Toronto Notes attributes to elevated ICP. Toronto Notes states that patients with suspected elevated ICP require urgent CT or MRI to identify the etiology and to assess for midline shift and herniation.

optionExplanations.b: LP before imaging is hazardous with suspected raised ICP because it can precipitate tonsillar and uncal herniation.
optionExplanations.c: Perimetry may document the enlarged blind spot but does not identify the underlying intracranial cause.
optionExplanations.d: EEG has no role in identifying a structural cause of raised ICP.
optionExplanations.e: Carotid Doppler assesses extracranial carotid disease and would not explain papilledema or an abducens palsy.

source.reference: NS7 — Clinical Features of Elevated ICP and Investigations (Table 4)

questions.question: A 22-year-old man is struck in the left temple by a baseball. He is briefly unconscious, then walks and converses normally for about two hours. He subsequently becomes progressively obtunded, with a dilated non-reactive left pupil and right-sided weakness. Non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense lenticular collection with sharp margins overlying the left temporoparietal region that does not cross suture lines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes the classic epidural hematoma sequence as post-traumatic reduced level of consciousness, a lucid interval of several hours, then obtundation, hemiparesis, ipsilateral pupillary dilation, and coma; 85% follow a temporal-parietal skull fracture tearing the middle meningeal artery. On non-contrast CT the clot is lenticular-shaped and usually limited by suture lines. This young man's lucid interval, ipsilateral pupillary dilation, contralateral hemiparesis, and lenticular clot fit that picture.

optionExplanations.a: Acute subdural hematoma classically has no lucid interval and appears as a hyperdense crescentic mass that crosses suture lines.
optionExplanations.b: Chronic subdural hematoma occurs 15 or more days after bleeding, typically in older or anticoagulated patients, and is hypodense and crescentic on CT.
optionExplanations.d: Subarachnoid hemorrhage shows hyperdense blood in the cisterns and fissures rather than a lenticular extra-axial collection.
optionExplanations.e: Diffuse axonal injury causes decreased level of consciousness with no space-occupying lesion visible on CT.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman presents 30 hours after the abrupt onset of the worst headache of her life, which peaked instantly while she was gardening. She continues to have neck pain and photophobia. She is fully alert with no focal neurological deficit. A non-contrast CT of the head performed on arrival is reported as normal. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Lumbar puncture for opening pressure, red blood cell count, and xanthochromia
Repeat non-contrast CT of the head in 24 hours
Discharge with analgesia and outpatient follow-up

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that non-contrast CT is 98% sensitive for subarachnoid hemorrhage within 12 hours and 93% within 24 hours, and may be negative with a small bleed or delayed presentation. When CT is negative but suspicion remains high, lumbar puncture is the highly sensitive next test, showing elevated opening pressure, an RBC count usually above 100000/mm3 that does not fall from first to last tube, and a xanthochromic supernatant by about 12 hours that lasts two weeks. This patient presented at 30 hours with a classic thunderclap headache, so a negative CT cannot exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage.

optionExplanations.b: CT sensitivity falls further with time, so a repeat scan the following day would be even less informative than the first.
optionExplanations.c: Discharge would miss a sentinel bleed, which precedes full-blown subarachnoid hemorrhage in 30-60% of patients within the preceding three weeks.
optionExplanations.d: Nimodipine is given for delayed cerebral ischemia neuroprotection once subarachnoid hemorrhage is confirmed; it is not a diagnostic step.
optionExplanations.e: MRI is not the listed diagnostic pathway for CT-negative suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage; lumbar puncture is the highly sensitive confirmatory test.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man develops severe low back pain radiating down both legs after lifting a heavy box. Over the following several hours he becomes unable to void and reports numbness over the perineum and inner thighs. Examination shows asymmetric weakness in multiple root distributions, absent ankle reflexes, and reduced anal sphincter tone. Which investigation is most appropriate?

options.text: Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine
Flexion-extension plain radiographs of the lumbar spine

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists urgent MRI as the investigation to confirm compression of the S2-S3-S4 nerve roots by a large disc herniation in suspected cauda equina syndrome. The syndrome usually develops in under 24 hours with weakness in multiple root distributions, reduced knee or ankle reflexes, urinary retention, and saddle (S2-S5) anesthesia. This presentation is typical, and surgical decompression within 48 hours is needed to preserve bowel, bladder, and sexual function.

optionExplanations.b: Plain films do not visualize the disc and nerve roots and would delay the decompression window.
optionExplanations.c: Electrodiagnostic studies do not localize acute compressive disc pathology and are not the urgent test here.
optionExplanations.d: A bone scan assesses bone turnover, not the soft tissue compression of the lumbosacral roots.
optionExplanations.e: CSF analysis has no role in diagnosing compressive cauda equina syndrome and delays definitive imaging.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with a known non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma presents with abrupt onset of severe headache, rapidly worsening bitemporal visual loss, ophthalmoplegia, and reduced mental status. She is hypotensive. Urgent MRI shows acute expansion of the sellar mass with hemorrhage. Endocrine testing confirms panhypopituitarism. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Rapid corticosteroid administration with surgical decompression

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines pituitary apoplexy as sudden expansion of the pituitary mass due to hemorrhage or necrosis, presenting with abrupt headache, visual disturbance, ophthalmoplegia, reduced mental status, panhypopituitarism, and diabetes insipidus. The listed treatment for apoplexy is rapid corticosteroid administration plus surgical decompression. Corticosteroid replacement addresses the acute hypoadrenalism causing her hypotension while decompression protects vision.

optionExplanations.b: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used for prolactinomas, not for acute apoplexy.
optionExplanations.c: Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, is used for acromegaly from a GH-secreting adenoma.
optionExplanations.d: Ketoconazole inhibits cortisol production and is used in Cushing's disease; it would worsen this patient's adrenal insufficiency.
optionExplanations.e: Cyproheptadine is a serotonin and histamine antagonist used in Cushing's disease, not in apoplexy.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man is brought in by his daughter with a 9-month history of a slow, broad-based magnetic gait, urinary incontinence, and progressive forgetfulness. He is afebrile with no focal deficits. CT of the head shows enlarged ventricles without increased prominence of the cerebral sulci. Which investigation best determines whether he is likely to benefit from shunting?

options.text: Lumbar tap test with CSF removal and reassessment of gait
Repeat CT of the head in six months

questions.explanation: This is the classic Hakim triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus: magnetic gait ataxia with apraxia, incontinence, and subcortical dementia, with CT showing enlarged ventricles without prominent sulci. Toronto Notes states that ICP monitoring, for example by LP or EVD, may be used to investigate NPH and test the response to shunting (the lumbar tap test). Improvement after CSF removal supports proceeding to a shunt.

optionExplanations.b: Toronto Notes notes that radionuclide cisternography can test CSF flow and absorption rate but is unreliable.
optionExplanations.c: EEG assesses cortical electrical activity and does not predict shunt responsiveness.
optionExplanations.d: Cerebral angiography evaluates vascular lesions and has no role in assessing CSF dynamics here.
optionExplanations.e: Serial imaging alone would delay treatment and does not test the response to CSF diversion.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with known cervical spondylosis trips and falls forward down three steps, striking his forehead and hyperextending his neck. He has marked weakness of both hands and forearms with only mild weakness in both legs, patchy bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the upper limbs, preserved light touch, and urinary retention. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists central cord syndrome as the most common incomplete cord syndrome, caused by syringomyelia, tumours, or spinal hyperextension injury. It produces bilateral motor weakness with upper limb weakness greater than lower limb weakness, urinary retention, and a variable bilateral suspended sensory loss in which pain and temperature loss exceeds loss of vibration and proprioception. This man's hyperextension mechanism and arm-predominant deficit match that pattern.

optionExplanations.b: Anterior cord syndrome follows anterior spinal artery compression or occlusion and causes bilateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion with preserved vibration and proprioception, not an arm-predominant suspended deficit.
optionExplanations.c: Brown-Sequard results from hemisection of the cord, giving ipsilateral weakness and proprioceptive loss with contralateral pain and temperature loss.
optionExplanations.d: Posterior cord syndrome preserves motor function and causes bilateral loss of vibration, proprioception, and light touch with preserved pain and temperature.
optionExplanations.e: A complete lesion causes bilateral loss of motor, sensory, and autonomic function more than four segments below the injury, whereas this man retains substantial function.

source.reference: NS34 — Incomplete Spinal Cord Lesion Syndromes

questions.question: A 71-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after tripping on a curb and striking his head. There was a witnessed brief loss of consciousness. His GCS is 15 on arrival, he has not vomited, and his neurological examination is normal. Examination shows periorbital ecchymosis and a right-sided hemotympanum. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Non-contrast CT scan of the head
Cervical spine x-ray with T1 well visualized

questions.explanation: The Canadian CT Head Rule requires a CT head in minor head injury (witnessed loss of consciousness, definite amnesia, or witnessed disorientation with GCS 13-15) if any high-risk feature is present, including any sign of basal skull fracture (hemotympanum, raccoon eyes, CSF otorrhea/rhinorrhea, Battle's sign) and age 65 or older. This patient has both periorbital ecchymosis with hemotympanum and is 71, so CT of the head is indicated even though his GCS is 15.

optionExplanations.b: Basal skull fractures are not readily seen on x-ray; the diagnosis relies on clinical signs, and CT with bone window is the gold standard for skull fractures.
optionExplanations.c: MR imaging is not the emergency test used to decide imaging in minor head injury under the Canadian CT Head Rule.
optionExplanations.d: The C-spine must still be cleared, but plain films are not recommended over CT and would not address the intracranial injury his high-risk features predict.
optionExplanations.e: Lumbar puncture should never be done in head injury until raised intracranial pressure has been ruled out.

questions.question: An 81-year-old anticoagulated man is brought in by his daughter with six weeks of gradually worsening confusion, minor headache and light-headedness. He struck his head on a cupboard door about two months ago. He is afebrile with no focal weakness. Non-contrast CT shows a hypodense crescentic mass over the right convexity that crosses suture lines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic subdural hematoma arises from ruptured subarachnoid bridging vessels, typically in patients over 50, EtOH users and those who are anticoagulated. It presents with minor headache, confusion, light-headedness and signs of increased ICP, and CT shows a hypodense crescentic mass that crosses suture lines. Treatment is burr hole drainage, with craniotomy if it recurs.

optionExplanations.a: Epidural hematoma follows a middle meningeal bleed from a skull fracture and appears as a hyperdense lenticular mass with sharp margins usually limited by suture lines, with a lucid interval before loss of consciousness.
optionExplanations.b: Acute subdural hematoma is a hyperdense crescentic mass presenting soon after trauma with hemiparesis and pupillary changes, not weeks of confusion.
optionExplanations.d: Subarachnoid hemorrhage presents with sudden onset thunderclap headache and hyperdense blood in the cisterns and fissures.
optionExplanations.e: Intracerebral hemorrhage appears as a hyperdense intra-parenchymal collection, typically in a hypertensive patient with sudden focal deficit.

source.reference: NS20 — Comparison of Epidemiology and Etiology of Intracranial Bleeds

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman is on day 7 of admission for aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage; her aneurysm was coiled on day 1 and she had been alert and oriented since. This morning she is confused and drowsy with a new right pronator drift. She is afebrile, her serum sodium is normal, and repeat CT shows no new blood and no ventricular enlargement. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hyponatremia due to cerebral salt wasting

questions.explanation: Vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage begins 4-14 days post-SAH and peaks at 6-8 days, presenting as a new onset ischemic deficit: confusion, decreased LOC, and focal speech or motor deficit such as pronator drift. It is diagnosed clinically and/or with transcranial Doppler and can progress to delayed cerebral ischemia, infarct and death. Nimodipine 60 mg q4h for 21 days is the only validated neuroprotective agent.

optionExplanations.b: Rebleeding would be expected to show new blood on CT, and her aneurysm has already been coiled, which is the only prevention of rebleed.
optionExplanations.c: Post-SAH hydrocephalus is due to blood obstructing the arachnoid granulations and would show ventricular enlargement on CT.
optionExplanations.d: Hyponatremia from cerebral salt wasting is a recognized SAH complication, but her serum sodium is normal.
optionExplanations.e: Neurogenic pulmonary edema is a recognized SAH complication but causes respiratory compromise rather than a new focal neurological deficit.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man with long-standing hypertension develops a left hemiparesis that worsened over 40 minutes, with headache and vomiting. His GCS is 13 and his blood pressure is 215/115 mmHg. Non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense intra-parenchymal collection in the right putamen with no hydrocephalus. His INR is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Lower the mean arterial pressure by about 20% toward a target blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg
Give corticosteroids to control raised intracranial pressure
Proceed to immediate craniotomy with evacuation of the clot
Obtain a cerebral angiogram to rule out a vascular lesion

questions.explanation: For intracerebral hemorrhage the emergency department priority is to decrease MAP to the pre-morbid level or by about 20%, targeting a blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg, while checking PTT/INR and correcting any coagulopathy, with transfer to a neuro-ICU or stroke unit. His pressure is markedly elevated and his coagulation is normal, so blood pressure control is the immediate step.

optionExplanations.b: Corticosteroids should not be used for elevated intracranial pressure in intracerebral hemorrhage.
optionExplanations.c: Surgery is contraindicated for difficult locations such as the basal ganglia and thalamus, and this is a putaminal bleed without rapid deterioration.
optionExplanations.d: Angiography is not required in a patient over 45 with known hypertension and a putaminal bleed, where the yield is approximately zero.
optionExplanations.e: Levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis is part of medical management but does not address his acutely elevated blood pressure.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man describes 14 months of insidious neck pain radiating into both arms and progressive gait disturbance. He can no longer button his shirt and reports an electric sensation down his spine when he extends his neck. Examination shows decreased dexterity, lower extremity weakness and upper motor neuron signs. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Flexion/extension x-rays of the cervical spine
Anteroposterior and lateral x-rays of the cervical spine

questions.explanation: This is degenerative cervical myelopathy: insidious onset neck pain radiating into the arms, a Lhermitte's sign with neck extension, gait disturbance, decreased dexterity, lower extremity weakness and UMN signs. MRI is the most useful investigation for determining compression of the neural element, which is what drives the decision to decompress.

optionExplanations.b: CT is used for better determination of bony anatomy such as ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament, not for cord compression.
optionExplanations.c: Flexion/extension views assess alignment and instability but do not show the compressed neural element.
optionExplanations.d: Plain x-rays assess alignment and fractures only and cannot demonstrate spinal cord compression.
optionExplanations.e: EMG and nerve conduction studies are reserved for peripheral nerve investigation.

questions.question: A 43-year-old office worker has three weeks of right arm pain that is worse with neck extension and ipsilateral rotation, together with numbness of the middle finger. Examination shows mild triceps weakness and a diminished triceps reflex. There is no gait disturbance, no sign of myelopathy and no night pain. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Activity modification, NSAIDs and a physiotherapy program focused on strengthening core muscles
Strict bed rest for two weeks

questions.explanation: His findings localize to the C7 root, most commonly from a C6-C7 disc herniation, with arm pain worsened by neck extension and ipsilateral rotation and LMN signs. Nonsurgical treatment is first line: activity modification, patient education, physiotherapy focused on core strengthening, and analgesics, with NSAIDs being more efficacious. Ninety-five percent improve spontaneously in 4-8 weeks, and he has no surgical indication.

optionExplanations.b: Bed rest is not advised unless radicular symptoms are severe.
optionExplanations.c: Cervical manipulation should be avoided in cervical disc syndrome.
optionExplanations.d: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion is the usual surgical approach, but surgery requires intractable pain despite adequate conservative treatment for more than 3 months or a progressive neurological deficit.
optionExplanations.e: Posterior foraminotomy with discectomy is an alternative surgical option, but he has no indication for surgery at three weeks.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman has three months of headache, nausea and blurred vision, and examination shows bilateral papilledema. MRI shows enlarged temporal horns with ballooning frontal horns and an enlarged 3rd ventricle, a normal-sized 4th ventricle, and periventricular lucency. A stenosis of the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius is identified. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In obstructive hydrocephalus CSF circulation is blocked within the ventricular system proximal to the arachnoid granulations, and aqueductal stenosis is a classic acquired cause. Imaging shows ventricular enlargement proximal to the block — enlarged temporal horns, ballooning frontal horns, an enlarged 3rd ventricle — with periventricular hypodensity/lucency from transependymal migration of CSF. The normal 4th ventricle places the block at the aqueduct.

optionExplanations.b: In communicating hydrocephalus absorption is blocked at an extraventricular site, most often the arachnoid granulations, and all ventricles are dilated.
optionExplanations.c: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is persistent ventricular dilation in the context of normal CSF pressure, not an aqueductal block with papilledema.
optionExplanations.d: Hydrocephalus ex vacuo results from atrophy of surrounding brain tissue and shows enlarged ventricles and enlarged sulci.
optionExplanations.e: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is raised ICP with papilledema but without hydrocephalus, and requires normal neuroimaging.

questions.question: A 49-year-old woman describes six months of pulsatile tinnitus and headache with no history of trauma. Over the past month her left eye has become proptotic and red. Examination shows chemosis and an audible bruit over the orbit, and her visual acuity is preserved. Non-enhanced CT shows no hemorrhage. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dural fistulas connect dural arteries to dural veins or the dural sinus and frequently occur at the transverse and cavernous sinuses. Pulsatile tinnitus points to sigmoid or transverse sinus involvement, and carotid cavernous involvement classically produces proptosis, chemosis and bruits. Non-enhanced CT is used to rule out hemorrhage, and angiography remains the gold standard for diagnosis.

optionExplanations.b: An arteriovenous malformation is a tangle of abnormal vessels that typically presents with hemorrhage, seizures, mass effect or focal deficits rather than an orbital syndrome.
optionExplanations.c: Cavernous malformations present with seizures, progressive neurological deficit or minor hemorrhage and are diagnosed on gradient echo MRI.
optionExplanations.d: Venous angioma is another listed type of vascular malformation but does not produce the carotid cavernous picture of proptosis, chemosis and bruit.
optionExplanations.e: Capillary telangiectasia is also a listed vascular malformation, but the cavernous sinus syndrome described here is characteristic of a dural fistula.

source.reference: NS27 — Arteriovenous Malformations, Cavernous Malformations, and Dural Arteriovenous Fistulas

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman has eight weeks of headache that appears within minutes of standing and resolves on lying flat, accompanied by tinnitus and dizziness. She has had no dural puncture. MRI brain with contrast shows pachymeningeal enhancement and sagging of the brain with low cerebellar tonsils. Two weeks of bed rest, hydration and caffeine have not helped. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Surgical repair of the dural leak

questions.explanation: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension is low CSF pressure with postural headache secondary to a CSF leak in a patient with no recent dural puncture; MRI shows sagging of the brain with low cerebellar tonsils and pachymeningeal enhancement. Conservative management is bed rest, hydration, caffeine and possibly theophylline; when that fails, the epidural blood patch, in which 10-20 mL of autologous blood is injected into the epidural space, is the mainstay treatment.

optionExplanations.b: Bed rest and hydration are conservative measures that have already failed over two weeks.
optionExplanations.c: Caffeine is part of the conservative regimen she has already completed without benefit.
optionExplanations.d: Theophylline is only a possible addition to conservative management, not the mainstay treatment.
optionExplanations.e: Surgery is indicated only if epidural blood patches are ineffective and the site of the leak has been localized.

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman with known lung cancer and a good Karnofsky score reports two weeks of headache and mild left arm clumsiness. Contrast CT of the head shows three round, well-circumscribed, ring-enhancing lesions at the grey-white matter junction, each under 2 cm, with surrounding edema. Restaging shows her extracranial disease is stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for the intracranial lesions?

options.text: Stereotactic radiosurgery to the three lesions
Craniotomy and resection of all three lesions

questions.explanation: Brain metastases are the most common intracranial tumour in adults, spread hematogenously, and 80% are hemispheric at the grey-white matter junction where emboli lodge in terminal middle cerebral artery branches. For multiple lesions the source recommends whole brain radiotherapy when there are more than 10 lesions and stereotactic radiosurgery when there are fewer than 10. With three small lesions, SRS is preferred, and emerging evidence supports avoiding WBRT in favour of focal radiation to spare cognitive function.

optionExplanations.b: WBRT is reserved for multiple lesions numbering more than 10; emerging evidence supports avoidance of WBRT and use of focal radiation to spare cognitive functions.
optionExplanations.c: Surgical resection with radiation is reserved for a single or solitary lesion, or a dominant lesion with significant mass effect or symptoms, in carefully selected patients.
optionExplanations.d: The role of chemotherapy is limited because of poor penetration across the blood-brain barrier.
optionExplanations.e: Median survival without treatment once symptomatic is about one month, so observation is not appropriate in a symptomatic patient with good performance status.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man with two months of inadequately treated left otitis media and mastoiditis develops one week of worsening headache, decreasing level of consciousness and a right hemiparesis, followed by a generalized seizure. Temperature is 38.1°C and he has a leukocytosis. Contrast CT of the head shows a left temporal lesion with central low density, ring enhancement and surrounding edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A cerebral abscess is pus in brain substance surrounded by a tissue reaction with capsule formation, and on CT it shows central low density from pus, ring enhancement and surrounding edema. Contiguous spread from an adjacent infection such as otitis media, mastoiditis or sinusitis is one of the four routes of microbial access to the CNS, and Streptococcus is the most common pathogen. Focal neurological signs, headache with decreased level of consciousness, hemiparesis and seizures in 50% of cases, plus low-grade fever and leukocytosis, fit this presentation.

optionExplanations.b: Subdural empyema is a bacterial or fungal infection of the subdural space due to contiguous spread from bone or air sinus that progresses rapidly; it is not an intraparenchymal ring-enhancing mass with a capsule.
optionExplanations.c: Epidural abscess occupies the cranial or spinal epidural space and is associated with osteomyelitis rather than producing a lesion within the brain substance.
optionExplanations.d: Meningitis produces meningeal signs and fever without an intraparenchymal ring-enhancing collection.
optionExplanations.e: Ventriculitis is described as a complication of abscess rupture rather than the initial lesion.

questions.question: A 41-year-old warehouse worker has six weeks of low back pain followed by leg pain that is now worse than the back pain. The pain radiates down the lateral leg to the dorsal foot and is exacerbated by Valsalva. There is weakness of hallux extension, sensory change over the dorsal foot to the hallux, and normal patellar and Achilles reflexes. Straight leg raise reproduces the pain at 40°. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: L5 root compression from a posterolateral L4-L5 disc herniation
S1 root compression from a posterolateral L5-S1 disc herniation
L4 root compression from a posterolateral L3-L4 disc herniation
Cauda equina compression from a central disc herniation

questions.explanation: A posterolaterally herniated disc compresses the nerve root exiting below the level of the disc, so an L4-L5 herniation compresses the L5 root. L5 involvement gives a sciatic pain pattern, sensory change over the dorsal foot to the hallux, weakness of extensor hallucis longus (hallux extension) and a medial hamstrings reflex change, with the patellar and Achilles reflexes preserved. A straight leg raise positive at less than 60° suggests L5 or S1 root involvement.

optionExplanations.b: S1 involvement produces sensory change over the lateral foot, weakness of gastrocnemius and soleus (plantar flexion) and a depressed Achilles reflex.
optionExplanations.c: L4 involvement produces a femoral rather than sciatic pain pattern, medial leg sensory change, tibialis anterior (dorsiflexion) weakness and a depressed patellar reflex, and would be suggested by a positive femoral stretch test.
optionExplanations.d: Central herniation may cause cauda equina compression, but this patient has a single unilateral dermatomal and myotomal deficit without bowel or bladder involvement.
optionExplanations.e: Neurogenic claudication is initiated by standing or walking with slow relief on postural change, not the persistent radicular pain with a positive straight leg raise described here.

questions.question: A term newborn boy is delivered with a midline lumbosacral sac through which meningeal and neural tissue has herniated, with no skin covering the defect. He has flaccid weakness of both legs distal to the anatomic level and dribbling urinary incontinence. Head circumference is enlarged and cranial ultrasound shows ventriculomegaly. What is the most appropriate initial treatment of the back lesion?

options.text: Observation only, as this anomaly requires no treatment
Ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion with the back lesion left open
Repair deferred until the child is one year of age
Prolonged intravenous antibiotics without operative repair

questions.explanation: Herniation of meningeal and CNS tissue through a spinal defect with no skin covering is a myelomeningocele, a spina bifida aperta caused by primary failure of neural tube closure. It produces sensory and motor changes distal to the anatomic level, urinary and faecal incontinence, and hydrocephalus in 65-85% of patients. Treatment is surgical closure to preserve neurologic status and prevent CNS infections; operative mortality is close to 0% with 95% two-year survival.

optionExplanations.b: It is spina bifida occulta, with no visible exposure of meninges or neural tissue, that requires no treatment.
optionExplanations.c: Hydrocephalus occurs in 65-85% of these patients and may need CSF diversion, but leaving the exposed defect open does not preserve neurologic status or prevent CNS infection.
optionExplanations.d: Delaying repair leaves exposed neural tissue at risk of CNS infection and further neurologic loss; closure is done to preserve neurologic status.
optionExplanations.e: Antibiotics do not close the neural tube defect, and prevention of CNS infection here depends on surgical closure.

questions.question: A 61-year-old immunocompetent man has six weeks of progressive cognitive and behavioural change with a mild right hemiparesis, and reports blurred vision with floaters. Contrast MRI shows two intensely and homogeneously enhancing periventricular lesions with minimal edema and restriction on diffusion imaging. There is no systemic malignancy on staging. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: High-dose dexamethasone with repeat MRI in two weeks
Craniotomy and gross total resection of both lesions

questions.explanation: Intensely enhancing periventricular lesions with homogeneous enhancement, minimal edema and restricted diffusion from hypercellularity in an immunocompetent patient with cognitive and behavioural symptoms and ocular floaters suggest primary CNS lymphoma. The source states that confirmation is by stereotactic biopsy and histopathology, and that corticosteroids may prevent histopathological diagnosis, so they should be avoided until the biopsy is complete when clinically possible.

optionExplanations.b: Corticosteroids may prevent histopathological diagnosis and should be avoided until the biopsy is complete when clinically possible.
optionExplanations.c: Surgery is generally reserved for stereotactic biopsy in primary CNS lymphoma; resection is discouraged.
optionExplanations.d: Chemotherapy with the MATRix regimen is first-line treatment, but only after the diagnosis is confirmed by stereotactic biopsy and histopathology.
optionExplanations.e: Radiation is used for consolidation or palliation, or as second-line induction in patients ineligible for high-dose methotrexate, and does not substitute for tissue diagnosis.

source.reference: NS16 — Primary Central Nervous System Lymphoma

questions.question: A 34-year-old man reports two years of progressive pain, weakness and wasting of both hands. Examination shows loss of pain and temperature sensation in a band-like distribution over both shoulders and upper arms, with light touch and proprioception preserved. His right shoulder is swollen and deformed but painless. Leg strength and sensation are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Chiari I malformation without a syrinx

questions.explanation: Syringomyelia is cystic cavitation of the spinal cord that begins with pain and weakness and later produces atrophy and loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract) in the upper extremities from a central cervical syrinx. The sensory loss occurs in a band-like distribution at the level of the cervical syrinx with touch and proprioception preserved (dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway), and painless neuropathic arthropathies (Charcot's joints) develop, especially in the shoulder and neck, because of the lost pain and temperature sensation. This patient's dissociated band-like sensory loss, LMN hand wasting and painless destroyed shoulder are that picture; MRI is the best method of confirming it.

optionExplanations.b: Chiari I malformation is associated with 70% of syrinxes, but it is listed as the cause of the cavity rather than the lesion that produces band-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch.
optionExplanations.c: Tethered cord is one of the listed causes of a syrinx; on its own it does not generate the upper extremity dissociated sensory loss and Charcot's joints described here.
optionExplanations.d: Arachnoiditis causes non-communicating syringomyelia by disrupting CSF flow dynamics in the cord, so it is an underlying etiology rather than the lesion producing this cape-like pattern.
optionExplanations.e: Basilar invagination is associated with 10% of syrinxes but is a bony craniovertebral junction anomaly, not the intramedullary cavity responsible for these findings.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man dives into shallow water and strikes the crown of his head. He is alert and neurologically intact but has severe upper neck pain and tenderness. Open-mouth odontoid x-ray and CT show both lateral masses of C1 displaced outward, with the ring of the atlas disrupted at two points. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In a C1 vertebral (Jefferson) fracture, vertical compression forces the occipital condyles of the skull down on the C1 vertebra (atlas), pushing its lateral masses outward and disrupting its ring. Axial loading from a dive onto the crown of the head is exactly that mechanism, and outward displacement of both C1 lateral masses on the open-mouth view with a disrupted atlas ring is its radiographic signature. Imaging is AP spine x-ray (open-mouth and lateral view) and CT, and treatment is immobilization in a cervical collar or halo vest until healing occurs, usually 2-3 months.

optionExplanations.b: An odontoid fracture causes C1 and the odontoid of C2 to move independently of the C2 body; patients often report a feeling of instability and present holding their head with their hands, and the atlas ring is not split.
optionExplanations.c: A hangman fracture is a bilateral fracture through the pars interarticularis of C2 with subluxation of C2 on C3, not a burst of the C1 ring.
optionExplanations.d: A clay-shoveler fracture is an avulsion of a spinous process, usually C6 or C7, and would not displace the C1 lateral masses.
optionExplanations.e: Vertical compression can also cause an occipital condylar fracture, but on its own it does not disrupt the ring of the atlas or spread its lateral masses.
